questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of admission webhooks, namespace-scoped control, and per-namespace policy management. It also touches TLS, RBAC, and logging considerations in Kubernetes.

## Key Concepts
- ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with NamespaceSelector
- Per-namespace ConfigMap policy
- Pod securityContext checks (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
- TLS setup, CA trust, and logging to a PVC

## Code Example
```yaml
# webhook Deployment skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-security-webhook
  namespace: webhooks
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ns-security-webhook
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-security-webhook
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: ns-security-sa
      containers:
      - name: webhook
        image: myorg/ns-security-webhook:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8443
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /tls
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: ns-security-tls
```

```yaml
# ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with NamespaceSelector
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: ns-security-webhook-config
webhooks:
- name: ns-security.webhook.example.com
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: ns-security-webhook
      namespace: webhooks
      path: "/validate"
    caBundle: <base64-CA-cert>
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      webhook: enabled
  sideEffects: None
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle policy updates without redeploying the webhook?
- What are the performance implications of per-create admission checks?
- How would you test this in a CI pipeline?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical CKAD pattern: file-driven config synchronization, idempotent object creation, secret management, and namespace-scoped network policy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer tooling, kubectl in-cluster, ConfigMap/Secret management, TLS sidecar, NetworkPolicy scoping.
- Cadence-based reconciliation and minimal YAML skeletons for CKAD.

## Code Example
```javascript
# Minimal skeleton for a Deployment that performs config sync
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-sync
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-sync
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl kubectl"]
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: my-registry/config-sync:latest
          env:
            - name: SYNC_INTERVAL
              value: "300s"
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you secure the TLS sidecar and rotate certs without restarting pods?
- How would you test reconciliation and conflict resolution between file changes and cluster objects?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical handling of in-cluster secret management, file-watching, and safe API exposure.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes Secrets and RBAC
- InitContainers and sidecars
- In-cluster API calls with kubectl
- NetworkPolicy scoping and TLS rotation

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-rotator
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secret-rotator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secret-rotator
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: secrets
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: secrets-pvc
      containers:
        - name: rotator
          image: example/secret-rotator:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /secrets
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: rotator-creds
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache kubectl jq"]
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: reg-creds
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a one-off reconciliation Job that interacts with external services, ensures idempotent processing via a fingerprint, and properly configures InitContainers, Secrets, and backoff behavior. It also checks handling of PVC-mounted data and rollback planning.


## Key Concepts

- Kubernetes Job with backoff and deadline
- InitContainer for bootstrap tooling
- PVC mounting and data access in a one-off task
- yq for YAML extraction
- Idempotent design via server fingerprint key
- Secret and ConfigMap usage for credentials and endpoints
- Rollback and observability considerations


## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
spec:
  backoffLimit: 4
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
  template:
    metadata:
      name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reconciler
        image: your-registry/audit-client:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "set -e; /bin/reconcile.sh /data/manifests.yaml"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq && curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/yq https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/download/v4.9.6/yq_linux_amd64 && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/yq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: data-manifests
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
```


## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test idempotency in CI/CD?
- How would you scale this for larger manifest sets without timeouts?
- How would you monitor and rollback on failure?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: ConfigMap-driven rolling updates, lifecycle hooks, probes, resource limits, PDB, and NetworkPolicy in a real namespace-scoped workload.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap rollouts via checksum annotation
- Probes (readiness, liveness, startup)
- PodDisruptionBudget impact on maintenance
- NetworkPolicy egress scoping to a service
- PVCs and volume mounts in Deployments

## Code Example
```yaml
# Deployment skeleton (aggregator)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: aggregator
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: <CONFIGMAP_SHA>
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: aggregator
        image: your-image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data-input
          mountPath: /data/input
        - name: data-output
          mountPath: /data/output
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/aggregator
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
        startupProbe:
          tcpSocket:
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 20
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 12
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sleep", "5"]
      volumes:
      - name: data-input
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: input-pvc
      - name: data-output
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: output-pvc
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: aggregator-conf
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: aggregator-pdb
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: aggregator
```

```yaml
# NetworkPolicy skeleton (namespace analytics)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-analytics-egress
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: analytics
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: analytics-svc

    - protocol: TCP

```

- How would you test failure and rollback scenarios?
- How would HPA interact with the PDB during a maintenance window?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to operate within a namespace context while working with core Kubernetes primitives: ConfigMaps for configuration, Secrets for sensitive data, and a controller-like process to automate cleanup tasks. It also assesses knowledge of observability (logging to PVC), container tooling (InitContainers), health checks, and network security.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped RBAC for job listing and deletion
- ConfigMap-driven TTL configuration
- Secrets for API key storage
- Kubernetes API access patterns (list, watch, delete Jobs)
- PVC-backed logging
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Readiness and liveness probes
- NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Trade-offs
- **Per-namespace vs. cluster-wide**: A per-namespace deployment provides isolation and TTL flexibility per namespace but increases resource overhead. A cluster-wide operator is more efficient but less flexible.
- **Polling vs. watching**: Polling is simpler to implement but introduces latency; watching is more efficient but adds complexity.
- **Push vs. pull for digests**: Sending digests immediately provides real-time visibility but increases API calls; batching reduces load but delays information.

## Why This Is Asked

- Ephemeral per-image Jobs

- Per-image status in a ConfigMap (scan-status)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress to vuln DB/scanner API

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: CronJob in audit namespace
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-scan-cron
  namespace: audit
spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          serviceAccountName: audit-scan-sa
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: image-scan-logs
          containers:
            - name: scanner
              image: registry.example/scanner:latest
              command: ["bash","-c","/usr/local/bin/scan.sh"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
```

kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-token
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fetch-token
        image: curl:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS https://vault.local/token -o /tokens/token.txt"]

      - name: token-vol

---
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: rotate-token
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"

            volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /secret
              name: secret-vol
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: secret-vol

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design Kubernetes-native backup patterns using CRD + Job orchestration, with proper use of InitContainers, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVs. Encourages thinking about per-namespace scoping, fault-tolerance, and minimal operator logic.

## Key Concepts
- CustomResourceDefinition and a namespace-scoped controller
- Jobs, InitContainers, and data packaging (tarball) for backups
- Secrets for credentials and ConfigMaps for configuration
- PVC usage for temporary/log data and readiness/liveness probes
- Idempotency, retries, and failure semantics

## Trade-offs Discussion

**Advantages:**
- Namespace isolation prevents cross-namespace interference
- Job-based approach provides built-in retry and failure handling
- InitContainers ensure dependencies are met before main workload
- Readiness/liveness probes provide operational visibility
- Secret/ConfigMap separation follows security best practices

**Limitations:**
- Requires custom controller for CRD watching and Job creation
- No incremental backup support (full tarball each time)
- AWS credentials stored in cluster (consider IRSA/EKS)
- No backup verification or restore automation
- PVC mounting requires proper permissions and access

**Alternatives:**
- Use Velero for comprehensive backup/restore solution
- Implement CSI snapshot for instant PVC backups
- Consider sidecar pattern for continuous backup
- Use CronJob instead of one-time Jobs for scheduled backups

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Explores per-namespace data ingestion, config-driven parsing, and strict egress controls—core CKAD topics with practical trade-offs.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps for runtime parsing rules
- PVC-backed logs and InitContainers for tooling
- Secrets for credentials and tokens
- TLS sidecar and cert rotation
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: Deployment, PVC, ConfigMap/Secret refs
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-router
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-router
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-router
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c","apk add --no-cache awk sed curl"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: router
        image: myorg/log-router:latest
        env:
        - name: REGEX
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: log-config
              key: regex
        - name: BATCH_SIZE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: log-config
              key: batchSize
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs-pvc
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: log-tls
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the regex parsing and batching in a SRP-safe way?
- What metrics would you expose for reliability and observability?

## Why This Is Asked

This tests converting a real-world requirement into Kubernetes manifests and basic operational steps, including probes and config injection.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment and ReplicaSet lifecycle
- Readiness and liveness probes
- ConfigMap-based configuration
- Service exposure and ports

## Code Example

```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myregistry/api:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-svc
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you extend configuration with Secrets for sensitive data?
- How would you monitor readiness/liveness in a multi-container pod?
